issues.legal_issue: Property within the temple compounds and included in the statutory record of the temple forms part of the temple under the governing statutory definition.
material_facts: The disputed rooms stood on a plot between the temple’s inner and outer compounds, with access through the temple’s main gate.
The statutory record of rights and premises included the plot within the temple area.
issues.conclusion: The disputed premises formed part of the temple.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(d) of the Puri Shri Jagannath Temple (Administration) Act, 1952, defines the temple to include its premises and appurtenant places. The Court relied on the record prepared under section 3, whose entries were final under section 5 except through the prescribed procedure, and on the record’s inclusion of the disputed plot within the temple premises.

predicates.temple_property_scope_dispute: A dispute arose over whether property fell within the statutory definition of a temple.
predicates.property_recorded_within_temple: The official record prepared for the temple included the property within the temple premises.
predicates.property_within_temple_compounds: The property was situated within the temple’s compounds or premises.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns the scope of a temple and the official record includes property situated within the temple premises, the property forms part of the temple.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a grant creates a lease or a licence depends on its substance and the parties’ intention, not merely on the form of the document or the fact of occupation.
material_facts: The grant permitted the grantee to open a store room but did not precisely identify the plot or create an interest in it.
The temple retained control of the premises, including a right of entry; the premises were inaccessible to the occupant during part of each night, and temple employees cleaned the area.
The grant did not give the grantee exclusive possession of the premises.
issues.conclusion: The grant created a licence, not a lease.
issues.legal_principle: Section 105 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, defines a lease, and section 52 of the Easements Act, 1882, defines a licence. The controlling test is whether the grant creates an interest in immovable property, assessed from its substance and the parties’ intention. Exclusive possession is prima facie evidence of a tenancy but is not conclusive if the circumstances negate an intention to create one. The Court relied on Associated Hotels of India Ltd. v. R.N. Kapoor, Quadrat Ullah v. Municipal Board, Bareilly, Board of Revenue v. A.M. Ansari, Errington v. Errington, Cobb v. Lane, and M.N. Chubwala v. Eide Hussain Sahib.

rule.if: lease_or_licence_characterization_dispute and grant_only_permitted_limited_use and owner_retained_control and occupant_lacked_exclusive_possession

predicates.lease_or_licence_characterization_disput: A dispute arose over whether an instrument granting use of premises created a lease or a licence.
predicates.grant_only_permitted_limited_use: The instrument permitted a specified use of the premises without granting an interest in them.
predicates.owner_retained_control: The owner or its representatives retained control over the premises.
predicates.occupant_lacked_exclusive_possession: The occupant did not have exclusive possession of the premises.

issues.definition: If a grant characterization dispute concerns permission for a limited use while the owner retains control and the occupant lacks exclusive possession, the grant is a licence rather than a lease.

issues.legal_issue: A manager of religious endowment property cannot grant a permanent lease without legal necessity or benefit to the estate.
material_facts: The grant was made by the temple’s manager, whose position was that of a shebait.
The grant was claimed to be permanent and for a fixed rent.
No legal necessity or benefit to the temple estate was proved.
issues.conclusion: Even if the grant were a lease, it was invalid as a permanent lease of the temple property.
issues.legal_principle: Under Hindu law, a shebait or manager may alienate endowment property only for legal necessity or the benefit of the estate and cannot, absent such justification, grant a permanent lease at a fixed rent. The Court relied on the principle in Hunooman Pershad v. Mussamat Babooee, Palaniappa Chetty v. Deivasikamony Pandara, and Shibessouree Debia v. Mothooranath Acharjo, and referred to Mulla’s Principles of Hindu Law and Mayne’s Treatise on Hindu Law.

rule.if: challenge_to_permanent_lease_of_religious_endowment and manager_granted_permanent_lease and no_legal_necessity and no_estate_benefit

predicates.challenge_to_permanent_lease_of_religiou: A dispute concerned the validity of a claimed permanent lease of religious endowment property.
predicates.manager_granted_permanent_lease: The manager of the religious endowment purported to grant a permanent lease of its property.
predicates.no_legal_necessity: No legal necessity for the permanent lease was established.
predicates.no_estate_benefit: No benefit to the estate from the permanent lease was established.

issues.definition: If a manager purports to grant a permanent lease of religious endowment property and neither legal necessity nor benefit to the estate is established, the permanent lease is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A grant permitting the use of premises as a store room does not itself confer a right to sell religious offerings there when the grant does not authorize that activity.
material_facts: The grant permitted the opening of a store room for the stated purpose of storing articles for preparation of the deities’ offering.
The grant did not confer a right to sell dry religious offerings.
A separate document relied on by the claimant concerned a different offering and did not establish a right to sell dry offerings.
issues.conclusion: The grant did not confer a right to sell dry religious offerings in the premises.
issues.legal_principle: The rights conferred by a grant are determined by its terms and substance. The Court found that the grant authorized opening a store room for its stated purpose but did not authorize sale, and that the separate document relied on concerned a different offering.

predicates.injunction_claim_based_on_grant: A claimant sought an injunction based on rights said to arise from a grant of premises.
predicates.grant_authorized_storage_only: The grant permitted storage or use as a store room but did not extend beyond that stated purpose.
predicates.grant_did_not_authorize_sales: The grant did not authorize the sale of the relevant goods or offerings on the premises.

issues.definition: When an injunction claim relies on a grant limited to storage that does not authorize sales, the grant confers no right to sell on the premises.
